blocks.content: You have probably already seen an address written like 192.168.1.0/24 somewhere, in a router settings page, a cloud provider dashboard, or a networking diagram. That trailing slash and number is CIDR notation, and once you understand what it actually means, a whole category of networking configuration suddenly makes sense.

CIDR, Classless Inter Domain Routing, is the standard way modern networks describe a whole range of IP addresses using one compact piece of notation, rather than listing every single address out individually.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541162-808408124.png
1. The Problem CIDR Actually Solves

Long before CIDR, IP addresses were divided into a small number of rigid, fixed size classes, Class A, Class B, Class C, each one a fixed, predetermined block size. This was genuinely wasteful: an organization needing a bit more than a small Class C block was often handed an enormous Class B block instead, wasting a huge number of addresses that organization would never actually use.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541163-279656382.png

CIDR fixed this by letting a network be described as exactly the size it actually needs, not forced into one of a few rigid, predetermined sizes. This is directly why it is called classless, it does away with the old rigid class system entirely.
2. Reading CIDR Notation: The Prefix Length
blocks.text: 2. Reading CIDR Notation: The Prefix Length

blocks.content: An IPv4 address has 32 total bits. The number after the slash in CIDR notation, called the prefix length, says exactly how many of those 32 bits are fixed and shared across the whole network, the network part. The remaining bits are free to vary from one device to the next within that network, the host part.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541163-391530744.png
blocks.alt: Reading CIDR Notation: The Prefix Length

blocks.content: 3. A Worked Example: /24

Take 192.168.1.0/24. The /24 says the first 24 bits are fixed, which corresponds exactly to the first three of the four numbers, 192.168.1. The remaining 8 bits are free to vary, giving 256 possible addresses in total, from 192.168.1.0 all the way through 192.168.1.255.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541163-258847401.png
4. A Worked Example: /16
Take 10.0.0.0/16. The /16 says only the first 16 bits are fixed, corresponding to the first two numbers, 10.0. The remaining 16 bits are free to vary, giving a much larger 65536 possible addresses.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541687-670265145.png
5. The Core Rule: Smaller Number Means Bigger Block
blocks.text: 5. The Core Rule: Smaller Number Means Bigger Block

blocks.content: This trips people up at first, but it makes sense once you see the mechanism. A SMALLER number after the slash means fewer bits are fixed, leaving MORE bits free to vary, which means a BIGGER block of addresses. A LARGER number after the slash means more bits are fixed, leaving fewer free, which means a SMALLER, more precise block.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541688-676889571.png
blocks.alt: The Core Rule: Smaller Number Means Bigger Block

blocks.title: The rule stated once more, clearly
blocks.content: Prefix length and block size move in opposite directions. Fewer fixed bits, /16 for instance, means a larger block. More fixed bits, /24 for instance, means a smaller block.
6. Why This Matters for Real Routers
blocks.text: 6. Why This Matters for Real Routers

blocks.content: CIDR is not just a convenient shorthand for humans, it is genuinely central to how real routers work efficiently at internet scale. One single CIDR entry in a router routing table can represent an entire block of thousands, even millions, of individual addresses, dramatically smaller and more efficient than a table that had to list every single address one by one, tying directly forward to the routing fundamentals topic later in this module.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541688-756956193.png
blocks.alt: Why This Matters for Real Routers

blocks.content: 7. Real World Examples You Will Actually See
blocks.text: 7. Real World Examples You Will Actually See

blocks.content: A typical home network is commonly a /24, giving 256 addresses, more than enough for any home. A cloud provider handing your team a large private network block might use something like a /16, giving tens of thousands of addresses for a big, growing set of servers. A single, specific address, like the well known public DNS server 8.8.8.8, is sometimes written as /32, meaning every single bit is fixed, a block of exactly one address.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541688-689828021.png

blocks.title: This is exactly what the sibling subnetting-basics topic builds on
blocks.content: CIDR gives you the notation for describing an address range. The subnetting-basics topic covers how to actually take one larger block and deliberately divide it into several smaller ones using this exact same notation.
